sections.name: Trolls
sections.card:
Summary: Big, ape-like brutes with three black eyes, claws that hit hard and a lot of health that comes back fast during a fight. The pale-furred frost trolls live farther north and higher up and are much tougher than the ordinary cave kind. Every troll leaves troll fat behind.
Weak points: Fire is their weak spot: it hurts them and slows their healing, though only for a while, and if you stop hitting them for long enough the healing goes back to normal. Lingering-damage poisons are a good stand-in when you have no fire. Paralysis helps too, because once it wears off a troll takes a long time to get back on its feet.
Looks like: A large, ape-like creature with three black eyes. Frost trolls have white fur.
Tips: Keep your health full: a short string of their blows can kill you, and they come in very quick succession. Hit-and-run works badly because they heal, so raise your armor and add fire by spell or enchantment; with several fire-enchanted weapons to pick from, a lighter, faster one may do better than a heavy one. A frost troll always waits on the snowy canyon path to High Hrothgar, whatever your level.

sections.name: Giants
sections.card:
Summary: Enormous humanoids met at their camps, where they herd mammoths. They leave you alone until you get too close or harm their mammoths, and they stay at level 32 however strong you are.
Weak points: A hostile giant will not walk into water and eventually wanders off if you stay in it, a weakness you can use when you are low level. Frost spells slow it, and the Unrelenting Force shout at full strength (all three words) can knock it down. Standing on a cliff it cannot reach helps you survive, and from a doorway it cannot enter you can pelt it with attacks.
Looks like: An enormous humanoid dressed in animal hides and furs, in one of three different looks.
Tips: A giant warns you first: it shakes its club overhead, then stomps the ground and turns hostile if you keep coming. Early on even a blocked blow can kill you, so dodge; you can sprint straight past a giant as it starts a club slam or a stomp, because those hits land in front of it and not in a wide circle. You can loot a giant's chest in front of it if you do not linger.

sections.name: Frostbite spiders
sections.card:
Summary: Giant spiders that attack on sight, in the wilds and in dungeons, usually in lairs hung with webs. Their poison hurts both health and stamina. The small ones are the easiest, then the medium ones, and the toughest are bigger than a horse.
Looks like: Reddish orange in dungeons and the south of Skyrim, bluish white in the north, ranging from small up to larger than a horse.
Tips: They spit venom from range, even when turned partly away from you, and leap in to bite; without poison resistance almost every hit poisons you. The biggest can outrun you on foot even at a sprint, so you would need a horse to get away. Two giant ones sometimes fight over a corpse in the wild, but if one survives or they spot you first they turn on you. They drop frostbite venom.

sections.name: Hagravens
sections.card:
Summary: Dangerous half-crone, half-bird creatures that claw you up close and cast destruction magic from afar, often area spells such as Fireball. They show up alone or in threes, often with the Forsworn or in hidden groves and lairs.
Weak points: Their claws are slow and simple to sidestep, and they turn and walk slowly, so a character of low level can win just by stepping back after each swing of their own. Ice-magic hagravens are the easier kind because they have no area spell.
Looks like: Part old crone, part bird.
Tips: A heavily armored warrior can charge in, since armor guards against their claws better than against their spells; with strong elemental resistance, keep your distance and use ranged attacks instead. A hagraven always drops hagraven feathers and sometimes a claw.

sections.name: Spriggans
sections.card:
Summary: Nature spirits that look like glowing green women, mostly wood. They heal themselves, call animals (even normally peaceful ones) to fight for them and summon insect swarms. They hide in foliage with an invisibility spell and strike as you pass, and some step out of tree trunks.
Weak points: Fire is their weakness. Their big self-heal seems to work only once a fight; just before and while they crouch to heal they resist most damage, so little lands until they get back up.
Looks like: A glowing green, woman-shaped figure that is mostly wood. Glowing insects around its body stay visible even when it turns invisible.
Tips: Its poison spray reaches much farther than a Flames spell and does more damage when cast with both hands. A green flash across the screen means it has called wildlife to fight you, and staggering it mid-cast does not stop that. Its loot is taproot.

sections.name: Dwarven spiders and Dwarven spheres
sections.card:
Summary: Two of the smaller machines met in Dwarven ruins. Spiders are small, agile and very common, often busy mining or repairing things. Spheres were built for combat: they patrol rolled up in a ball until they meet a threat, then unfold into a half-humanoid shape. Either kind can wait inside pipe ports in the walls and ceilings and spring out as you pass.
Weak points: Shock spells do normal damage to them, while frost and poison do nothing, and they turn aside a quarter of magic damage. Paralysis does not work on them. Unrelenting Force can knock a spider over; no other kind of automaton falls to it that way.
Looks like: Spiders are small and arachnid-like, and the stronger ones have electrical effects crackling from their core. A sphere rolls as a ball and rises into a half-humanoid shape to fight.
Tips: Spiders above level 7 fire short-range electric jolts and burst with more shock damage a moment after they die, and any spider can leap at you to close the gap. Higher-level spheres shoot darts from arm-mounted crossbows and lunge so fast they are hard to sidestep. Both kinds drop scraps, Dwarven oil and soul gems.

sections.name: Dwarven centurions
sections.card:
Summary: The biggest and strongest machines left in the Dwarven ruins, and usually the ruin's boss. A centurion hits as hard as a dragon can and has a steam breath that works like a shout. Most stand still in a charging gantry until you come near, a lever is pulled or you shoot them from range, and some are used as traps.
Weak points: Stand right against its legs: it cannot lower its arms or tilt its head to hit anything beneath its shoulders. Unrelenting Force staggers it, and used before it wakes it can leave the centurion inactive for a while so you can strike freely. Shock does normal damage, while frost and poison do not hurt it.
Looks like: A huge, heavily armored warrior shape: one arm ends in a hammer and the other in a battleaxe on a spring.
Tips: A ranged attacker gets a few shots in while it is still powering up. Or get it stuck outside a small hallway, stay out of its steam range and shoot or cast at it from there. Its remains hold a guaranteed Centurion Dynamo Core, plus a grand soul gem, Dwarven scraps, arrows and a few gems.

sections.name: Chaurus
sections.card:
Summary: Medium to large earwig-like creatures of swamps, marshes and deep caverns, often kept by Falmer for their chitin. They spit a strong acidic poison that quickly eats through most armor, they climb walls and they have lots of health.
Weak points: They avoid crossing water, even knee-deep, so arrows and spells from range work well. Their poison lands less often when you fight them up close, so melee is a sound plan.
Looks like: An earwig-like insect, medium to large in size.
Tips: A resist-poison effect only helps if you apply it before the poison damage begins, so carry cure poison potions and use one quickly after a hit. You can also coat your own weapon with poisons, especially ones that weaken, slow or paralyse the target. The poison keeps working after the chaurus is dead, so watch your health. You cannot eat chaurus, and the chitin they drop is used only in smithing.

sections.name: Ice wraiths
sections.card:
Summary: Hostile frost spirits that fly fast, circle you and hit with strong frost attacks. They live in cold, snowy places, often in Winterhold and the Pale, and are drawn to standing stones and Nordic ruins.
Weak points: Fire hurts them extra, and Dawnbreaker and Turn Undead also work on them. Frost does nothing to them, since they resist it fully.
Looks like: Wispy, flying spirits of frost.
Tips: A bite drains stamina, about 21 over three seconds. They also cast a weak wall of frost when attacking or closing in on you, but not while wandering or moving away. They ignore the terrain and can get stuck, or even die, on high ground. Even though they fly, they set off runes. They drop ice wraith teeth and essence.

sections.name: Flame, frost and storm atronachs
sections.card:
Summary: Elemental Daedra that you often meet when an enemy spellcaster has called them up, though you can conjure them too. None of the three kinds can be paralysed, raised as undead servants or turned invisible.
Looks like: Flame atronachs look like women made of fire in black metal armor. Frost atronachs are oversized humanoids of solid ice. Storm atronachs are the pieces of a shattered statue circling an unseen, electrified centre.
Tips: The flame atronach is the weakest of the three and very agile: it prefers to cast fire from a distance and tries to avoid melee. The frost atronach has a long reach and usually staggers you, but it has no ranged attack, and once you are in reach its chilling cloak slows you. Storm and flame atronachs hover, so they can walk on water. Unbound ones leave fire, frost or void salts. You cannot soul-trap atronachs you summoned yourself, but you can trap another caster's.

sections.name: Forsworn Briarhearts
sections.card:
Summary: The boss-level fighters among the Forsworn, a clan of Reachmen, found wherever the Forsworn set up camp. A Briarheart can be a dangerous spellcaster or a melee fighter, and every one is a man.
Weak points: A Briarheart dies at once if you steal its Briar Heart with pickpocketing.
Looks like: A man with a Briar Heart crudely set into his chest cavity and held there by leather straps, in a special kind of Forsworn armor with boots and a headdress.
Tips: They often have unusually keen hearing, so sneaking up on one is hard. They count as living, not undead: undead-only spells do not affect them, silver weapons gain no bonus against them, and Detect Life finds them where Detect Dead does not.

sections.name: Soul gems
sections.card:
Summary: Items that capture the souls of creatures as they die. Once filled, a gem is the power source for enchanting and for recharging enchanted weapons. There are five standard sizes, the smallest petty and the largest grand, and some special kinds.
Uses: A filled gem powers a custom enchantment when you make it, or recharges a weapon whose enchantment has run down. The standard sizes are petty, lesser, common, greater and grand. Only a black soul gem, or the Black Star, can hold a human soul, and that soul always counts as grand.
Tips: If the game says your gem is too small although an empty grand gem is in your pack, you are after a human soul, which needs a black soul gem. Geode veins in Blackreach, and only there, yield two or three empty gems of any size each; grand and black ones start to appear at level 16 and are at their most likely from level 31. Azura's Star holds as much as a grand gem and is not used up.

sections.name: Ebony
sections.card:
Summary: A very hard, long-lasting black material, like glass in look, that smiths turn into fine armor and weapons.
Uses: Working ebony needs a Smithing skill of 80. Smelting two ebony ores gives one ingot, and mining a vein gives three ores. Armor from it is a level 32 heavy set and weapons are level 36, both built from leather strips and ebony ingots.
Tips: Narzulbur, an Orc stronghold, holds the main ebony mine, called Gloombound Mine. Falmer loot can hold ore from level 13, blacksmiths may stock ingots from level 27, general goods merchants may too from level 14, and an ingot now and then turns up in a chest.

sections.name: Dragonscale and Dragonplate armor
sections.card:
Summary: Top-tier armor made from dragon parts: light Dragonscale and heavy Dragonplate. Dragonscale is the top light armor of the base game, and among heavy sets only Daedric armor beats Dragonplate.
Uses: To craft either set you need a perk called Dragon Armor, the last one in the Smithing tree. It asks for Smithing 100 and every perk in one of the two armor branches, light or heavy, and it also doubles how much you improve dragon items. Both sets are level 38 and show up at vendors at that level, and their stats are below Daedric armor.
Tips: Each Dragonscale piece is tempered with one dragon scale. In Dragonplate, the cuirass and shield take one dragon bone, and the other three pieces (boots, gauntlets, helmet) are tempered with one dragon scale. A shrine of Akatosh on a hill northeast of Rorikstead holds one dragon scale that comes back every 10 in-game days, so you can start crafting before dragons appear in the world.
